speaker: shannonprice
text: This is a case about the function and separation of powers in local government, where Mr. Brinkman has sued the solicitor's office for failing to exercise a power that, according to him, we don't even have. The trial court's reading of the charter and the statutes at issue here works absurd results, and we ask this court to reverse for three reasons. First, because the broad language of the Cincinnati City Charter grants the solicitor an administrative authority to file suit. Second, because the state statutes at issue here, when construed properly and in their context, support this authority. And third, because the Cincinnati City Manager, who is under the charter the highest executive authority for the city, approved this specific lawsuit pre-filing. Now let's start with the language of the charter. The relevant provision is housed in Article 4, titled Executive and Administrative Services. It reads that the solicitor shall serve the mayor, council, officers, and boards of the city as legal counsel and attorney, and shall represent the city in all proceedings in court. The language we really need to hone in on here is to serve the city as legal counsel and attorney. There's no distinction in that language between serving as legal counsel by initiating suit and serving as legal counsel by defending suit, and for good reason, because in practical reality, to serve as effective legal counsel, the solicitor has to do both of those things. And that dual authority is contemplated by the state statutes here. The trial court honed in on 733.53, under which the city council may, if it chooses, direct the solicitor to file suit or defend suit in certain circumstances. But where the trial court made a mistake is in ignoring the language of other state statutes, including RC733.56, .57, and .58. These statutes, each of these statutes, imposes a mandatory duty on the solicitor. The solicitor shall file suit if one of these things occurs. But they make no mention of the legislative authority of the city. And that's because the legislative authority of the city doesn't have to provide pre-approval for the solicitor to defend the city's already existing rights. And that's what we did in this case. This case is about a constitutional challenge to RC9.68. Specifically, we were challenging whether or not the statute was in violation of the city's home rule authority. This home rule authority exists independently of any action by counsel. It has to. It comes from the Ohio Constitution itself. And the solicitor is tasked to defend the city's constitutional rights, among other interests. We have to be able to bring this type of suit when counsel is in recess, when counsel is divided, when, for example, there might be tension between the counsel and the manager or the counsel and the mayor. It is the role of the administrative branch and of an administrative authority, like the solicitor, to step in in these situations and to protect the city's legal interests. And that's what we did here.

We have checks and balances here. We have a removal power that has traditionally been, at all levels of government, the way that the legislature keeps an eye on the executive and the administrative. But what happened here was that the solicitor got explicit approval from the city manager to file this suit. And then it was filed. There's no dispute in the record that that is the procedure that we undertook. And that alone is enough to justify reversal of the trial court, which failed to consider the issue of the city manager's involvement at all. As for 733.53, this is where we need to start looking at the Ohio Supreme Court precedent in State Exera Toledo. Yes, the language in the Cincinnati City Charter is different than the language in the Toledo City Charter. But the language interpreted by the Toledo court is actually identical to the language in RC 733.53. The State Exera Toledo court interpreted that language to prosecute or defend broadly. I'd also like to return to another point you made, Judge Bach, about prior lawsuits. The trial court and Mr. Brinkman both cite to a specific 1999 lawsuit. That's the Winburn suit, where counsel and the solicitor worked in tandem to bring a politically very significant suit. But tellingly, counsel can't cite to any more recent suits where this happened. One case from 1999, where the city followed one specific procedure, does not create a legal imperative for the solicitor in all circumstances. Sometimes it makes sense from a political standpoint for the solicitor, the manager, the mayor, and counsel to make a public statement that they are all on board for pursuing a particular type of litigation. But that political reality doesn't change the language of the charter, doesn't change the language of the statutes. And neither the charter nor the statutes require us to get counsel approval before filing suit. Much has been made in the briefs and in the argument today about the supposedly unlimited authority at issue in this case for the solicitor. And that just isn't the city's argument. We don't have unlimited authority, because we are subject to supervision and removal ultimately by the manager, the mayor, and counsel. Rather, the city is arguing, and the solicitor is arguing, that we possess discretionary authority to enforce the laws as we see them. And if the manager doesn't like how we're doing it, the manager can remove the solicitor. If the counsel doesn't like how the manager and the solicitor are proceeding, then the counsel can move to remove the manager. There's no unlimited authority here. It's simply not at issue. Rather, what is at issue is the proper separation of powers between the legislative authority, which is one, but not the only, client of the solicitor, and the executive branch. As for principles of statutory construction, we just cannot emphasize enough the absurd results that the trial court's construction would work for other state statutes at issue in this case. The trial court honed in on 733.53, and it interpreted that statute to impose a mandatory duty, despite the absence of language in the statute that actually does so. The solicitor has to have this administrative authority to initiate suit in order for the taxpayer statutes to work. Yes, we're not often going to choose to sue ourselves, as counsel suggests, but there is that mandatory duty there.
